title: Trump Restores Schedule F Classification for Policy-Influencing Federal Jobs
description_short: OPM says Schedule Policy/Career covers certain merit-based career positions that influence federal policy.
description_medium: A January 20, 2025, executive order created the Schedule Policy/Career category for career federal roles involving confidential, policy-determining, policymaking, or policy-advocating work. The Office of Personnel Management says these positions remain career-based and merit-filled, rather than political appointments. Its guidance does not establish that 50,000 employees were purged or chosen as political enemies.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14171, which the Office of Personnel Management says created the Schedule Policy/Career category. OPM describes it as an excepted-service classification for career, nonpolitical positions that are confidential, policy-determining, policymaking, or policy-advocating. The agency says covered positions remain career-based and are filled on merit; they are not political appointments. OPM’s page sets out the category and its implementing guidance, including later rules, rather than a count of workers who were transferred or dismissed. It does not document a purge of 50,000 employees or show that named workers were selected because they opposed Trump. The policy changes the classification used for some jobs, and its effect on protections should be described through the order and final rule. The source therefore supports a change to the federal personnel framework, while the original title’s claims of a completed mass purge and political targeting went beyond the evidence in this record.
notes: OPM confirms creation of Schedule Policy/Career under Executive Order 14171 for specified career policy-influencing roles and says they remain merit-based, nonpolitical positions. The revised title and descriptions remove the unsupported 50,000-person purge and political-enemy claims.

title: New York AG Secures Court Order: Trump to Pay $2 Million for Misuse of Trump Foundation Funds
description_short: New York AG Secures Court Order: Trump to Pay $2 Million for Misuse of Trump Foundation Funds
description_medium: On November 7, 2019, a New York court ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for using charitable assets to intervene in the 2016 presidential primaries. Trump admitted to personally misusing Foundation funds and agreed to restrictions on future charitable service. The Trump Foundation had been dissolved under court supervision in December 2018; the stored entry date of January 28, 2016 instead refers to a separate Iowa fundraiser.
description_long: New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on November 7, 2019, that a state court had ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for using Trump Foundation funds to influence the 2016 presidential primaries. Trump admitted to personally misusing charitable assets and agreed to restrictions on future charitable service. The Foundation had already been dissolved under court supervision in December 2018, with remaining assets distributed to charities. The case concerned a January 2016 Iowa fundraiser held while Trump skipped a Republican debate; the event raised about $2.8 million for the Foundation, according to the supplied correction record. That fundraiser and the later court order are related but distinct events nearly four years apart. The existing entry is dated January 28, 2016, while its title describes the 2019 judgment. This lane cannot change the stored date or split the fundraiser into its own entry, so the corrected account still requires a metadata update before it can be applied without leaving a date mismatch.

title: PBS Reported More Than 30,000 Federal Workers Fired by February 28, 2025
description_short: PBS’s Feb. 28 tally counted 30,000-plus known firings, excluding 7,000 planned SSA cuts.
description_medium: On February 28, 2025, PBS NewsHour’s Lisa Desjardins reported that her review of known mass firings found more than 30,000 federal workers had been fired in recent weeks. She said the figure did not include 7,000 Social Security Administration employees the agency intended to dismiss. The segment reported more cuts were forecast and described ongoing court challenges.
description_long: PBS NewsHour reported on February 28, 2025, that its correspondent Lisa Desjardins had counted more than 30,000 federal employees fired in known mass dismissals over the preceding weeks. Desjardins said her tally included about 1,200 recent firings at the National Weather Service and between 1,000 and 5,000 IRS dismissals during the prior week. She explicitly excluded 7,000 Social Security Administration employees who, according to her reporting, were expected to be fired but had not yet been included in the completed-dismissal total. The segment also described proposed Department of Defense emails requiring employees to report recent work and a Department of Education buyout offer. Desjardins said more cuts were forecast and that courts had largely sided with fired employees in cases so far, while noting one judge had found probationary-worker firings unlawful without yet blocking them. The report is a dated tally of known firings, not a final count of notices or a claim that 200,000 people had already been terminated. Its distinction between completed dismissals and planned cuts is preserved here.
notes: PBS NewsHour’s February 28, 2025 transcript reports 30,000-plus known completed firings and separately identifies 7,000 planned SSA cuts not included in that total. The revised title and descriptions preserve that dated distinction and do not repeat the unsupported 200,000 completed-termination figure.

title: Pizzagate Conspiracy, Armed Incident at Comet Ping Pong, and Michael G. Flynn Jr.’s Defense (2016)
description_short: CNN linked the false Pizzagate theory to an armed intrusion at Comet Ping Pong and Flynn Jr.’s later defense of it.
description_medium: In 2016, the false “Pizzagate” story alleged that Hillary Clinton and other Democrats ran a child-sex ring from Washington pizzeria Comet Ping Pong. CNN reported that Edgar Maddison Welch entered the restaurant with an assault rifle, saying he had come to investigate the claim. The article also quotes Michael G. Flynn defending the conspiracy online after the incident.
description_long: The “Pizzagate” conspiracy falsely cast Hillary Clinton and other senior Democrats as leaders of a child-sex trafficking ring operating through Comet Ping Pong, a Washington, D.C., pizzeria. CNN’s December 2016 report describes how Edgar Maddison Welch arrived at the restaurant carrying an assault rifle and told police he had traveled from North Carolina to investigate the story. Welch fired a weapon inside the restaurant; no one was reported injured. The incident brought the consequences of the false allegation into the physical space it targeted. CNN also situated Pizzagate within a wider information environment where conspiracy claims spread rapidly online and were repeated by prominent media figures. After the shooting, Michael G. Flynn, son of incoming national security adviser Michael Flynn, defended the theory on Twitter, writing that it would remain a story until proven false. His response kept the allegation in public circulation after an armed intrusion had exposed the risks of treating it as fact.

description_short: Emoluments Clause Violated From Day One — Foreign Governments Book Trump Hotels

title: Trump Lifts Russia Sanctions on Oleg Deripaska's Aluminum Company
description_short: Treasury delisted En+, Rusal, and EuroSibEnergo after ownership and governance changes, while keeping sanctions on Deripaska.
description_medium: On January 27, 2019, Treasury removed En+, Rusal, and EuroSibEnergo from the sanctions list after saying the companies reduced Oleg Deripaska’s direct and indirect ownership and severed his control. Treasury cited independent board majorities, oversight, and expanded reporting requirements; it said sanctions on Deripaska himself remained in force.
description_long: On January 27, 2019, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control removed En+ Group, Rusal, and EuroSibEnergo from the sanctions list after notifying Congress in December. Treasury said the companies had reduced Oleg Deripaska’s direct and indirect ownership stakes and severed his control. Under the delisting terms, En+ and Rusal were to have boards with independent majorities, including U.S. and European directors with no business, professional, or family ties to Deripaska or another sanctioned person. Treasury also required ongoing audits, certification, and reporting, and said independent U.S. persons would vote a significant bloc of En+ shares. The announcement concerned the companies’ status, not Deripaska’s: Treasury explicitly said all sanctions on him remained in force. The official release documents the department’s stated basis for delisting and its governance conditions. It does not establish critics’ claims that Deripaska retained control through associates or that the decision was a political favor. Those claims require separate evidence and are not included in this account.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Lifts Russia Sanctions on Oleg Deripaska's Aluminum Company

notes: Treasury’s January 27, 2019 release confirms the three company delistings, the ownership and governance conditions, added audit and reporting requirements, and continued sanctions on Deripaska personally. The revised long description removes claims about political influence or continued control that the release does not substantiate.

title: Pardons Susan B. Anthony
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Susan B. Anthony as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Donald Trump pardoned Susan B. Anthony for an 1873 conviction for illegal voting. The Justice Department record lists a $100 fine and prosecution costs. Anthony had cast a ballot as part of the women’s suffrage movement; the supplied source confirms the conviction and pardon but gives no basis for treating the symbolic clemency as financial corruption.
description_long: The Justice Department’s pardon record lists Susan B. Anthony’s 1873 conviction for illegal voting in the Northern District of New York. The court imposed a $100 fine and the costs of prosecution. In 2020, Donald Trump granted her a posthumous presidential pardon. Anthony had voted in an era when women were denied the ballot, making the clemency a symbolic act connected to the history of women’s suffrage rather than a response to an ongoing criminal sentence. The DOJ record establishes the underlying conviction and fine, but it does not describe the public debate around the pardon or any reason Trump gave for issuing it. It also provides no evidence of a private benefit, political exchange or financial exploitation. The existing “Corrupt Pardons” classification is unsupported by the facts in this source. A fuller account could include the historical context and contemporary responses to the pardon, while clearly distinguishing that symbolic action from clemency grants involving current political allies or private interests.
